You express conditions and hypotheses with nuance: au cas où + conditional, à condition que / à moins que / pourvu que + subjunctive, si jamais, en admettant que.
provided that, as long as (+ subjunctive)
if only, it only takes (+ subjunctive)
to step back, get some perspective
Take a jumper, in case it gets cold.
I accept, on condition that I stay in Lyon.
We’ll leave tomorrow, unless it rains.
To use “au cas où” + conditional for an eventuality.
To express a condition with “à condition que”, “pourvu que”, “pour peu que” + subjunctive.
To express an exception with “à moins que (ne)” + subjunctive and “à moins de” + infinitive.
To make a hypothesis with “en admettant que”, “à supposer que” + subjunctive and with “si jamais”.
To weigh up a decision: peser le pour et le contre, prendre du recul.

Thursday, 15 May 2030. Julien, Ioana and Rose-Hélène are in a rented cottage in Cassis, near Marseille. In the evening, on the beach, while the little one sleeps in her pushchair, they finally talk about the ministry’s offer, as they had promised.
Right. It’s 15 May. We’re at the seaside. It was written in pen. So, talk.
I want to accept. But on condition that it changes nothing for us. I don’t want to become a father who spends his life on trains.
How many days a month would you travel?
Four or five, the first year. Unless the cities find their conductors themselves. In that case, I’d only go for the inaugurations.
And what if it doesn’t work? What if in a year the ministry changes its mind?
I asked for a guarantee: my post at the Conservatoire stays open for a year, in case I want to come back.
Théo and Lucia. As long as we trust them, they’ll do better than me. You saw Théo at the wedding.
I saw him. And I saw you watching him. Assuming you accept, when would you start?
On 1 July. And in October we’d plant the first lime trees. Lille, Marseille, Strasbourg… Odile wants to come to every planting, as long as we take the train.
Then I’ll tell you what I think. I weighed the pros and cons for three weeks. And there’s only one con.
You’ll be tired. And in a few months we’ll need you not to be.
(smiles and puts her hand on her belly) In case you hadn’t noticed, I haven’t drunk coffee for two weeks.
(“pour peu que” = as long as, if only)
(“il n’y a que” = there is only)
“Au cas où” expresses an EVENTUALITY you prepare for. Careful: it is followed by the CONDITIONAL, not the subjunctive!
My post stays open, in case I want to come back.
In case you hadn’t noticed… (past conditional, ironic)
“Au cas où” on its own, at the end, is very common in speech: “Prends un parapluie, au cas où.” = just in case.
2. Condition: à condition que, pourvu que, pour peu que
J’accepte, à condition que je reste à Lyon.
J’accepte, à condition de rester à Lyon.
Odile viendra, pourvu qu’on prenne le train.
Pour peu qu’on leur fasse confiance, ils réussiront.
“Pourvu que” alone at the start of a sentence expresses a strong hope: “Pourvu que ce soit une fille !” = Let’s hope it’s a girl!
“À moins que” = unless. It takes the subjunctive and, in careful French, an expletive “ne” (with no negative meaning):
I’ll go, unless the cities find their conductors.
I won’t come, unless I’m invited. (à moins de + infinitive)
Trap: “à moins qu’il ne pleuve” does NOT mean “unless it doesn’t rain”. The “ne” is decorative. Meaning: if it rains, we don’t leave.
4. Hypothesis: en admettant que, à supposer que, si jamais
En admettant que tu acceptes, quand commencerais-tu ?
À supposer qu’il ait raison, que faisons-nous ?
Si jamais tu changes d’avis, appelle-moi.
Dans l’hypothèse où le projet échouerait…
“Si jamais” = “si” + a hint of improbability (“if by any chance…”). Grammatically it behaves like “si”: never future or conditional after it.
peser le pour et le contre
Assuming you accept, when would you start?
“Nous partirons, à moins qu’il ne pleuve.” If it rains…
Pourvu que ce soit une fille !
Au cas où ce serait une fille !
À moins que ce soit une fille !

On Tuesday 13 May, Julien, Ioana and Rose-Hélène took the train to Marseille. It was the same journey Ioana had made for the first time four years earlier, at Christmas, with two tickets Julien had given her for her birthday. She remembered it as if it were yesterday. She hardly spoke French back then, and she had been afraid the whole way of saying something silly.

This time it was Rose-Hélène saying silly things, in three languages at once, to all the passengers in the carriage. She was two years and two months old, and she had discovered that people smiled when she said “bonjour”, “bună” and “hola” one after the other. An old lady gave her a biscuit. A man in a suit gave her a pen. Julien had to give the pen back.

In Marseille they hired a small car to drive to Cassis, twenty kilometres away. The house they had booked was above the harbour, at the end of a lane so narrow that Julien had to fold in the mirrors. The owner, Mrs Giraud, a lady of at least eighty, was waiting on the doorstep with a basket of figs and a list of recommendations.

“Close the shutters properly in case the mistral gets up,” she said. “Don’t leave the little one alone on the terrace unless the gate is shut. And if you ever need anything at all, I’m just opposite.” Then she looked at Rose-Hélène and added, more gently: “Let’s hope it’s sunny for her. Is it her first time at the sea?”

The first evening, Mrs Giraud brought them a fish soup, “in case you’re too tired to cook”. She stayed an hour on the terrace. Her husband had been a fisherman in Cassis for fifty years. He had died at sea, on a day of mistral, when she was forty. She had never left the house. “That way,” she said, “if he comes back, he’ll know where to find me.”

Ioana thought of Hélène, who had waited all her life for a man who never came back. She thought of Odile, who had waited for Henri on every voyage. She told Mrs Giraud their story in a few sentences, and the old lady listened, nodding. “Sailors’ wives are all alike,” she said. “We know how to wait. It’s our only talent, but we all have it.”

It was her first time. The next morning they went down to the little beach by the harbour. Rose-Hélène stopped at the water’s edge, very serious, holding her father’s hand. A wave came and wet her feet. She let out a cry, stepped back three paces, and looked at the water with total suspicion, as if the sea had personally betrayed her.

Then a second wave came, smaller. This time Rose-Hélène didn’t step back. She watched the water surround her ankles, then go away, then come back. And she burst out laughing. For the next two hours it was impossible to get her out of the water. She took Henri’s harmonica out of her mother’s pocket and blew into it every time a wave arrived, as if to greet it.

In the afternoon, Julien built a sandcastle with his daughter. Rose-Hélène insisted it should have a window in the roof, “like Yanis’s hall”. Julien made a little hole at the top of the castle with his finger. Rose-Hélène examined it for a long time, then placed a shell in the middle. “That’s Hélène,” she explained. Nobody had ever spoken to her about Hélène that way. She had understood it all on her own.

“Henri would have liked that,” Ioana said, watching her. “A sailor playing the harmonica for the waves.” Julien didn’t answer. He was thinking of his own grandparents, Marcel and Rose, who had had a house by the sea in Marseille, and whom he had spent every childhood summer watching play the accordion and dance on the terrace. Rose-Hélène was named after his grandmother.

On Wednesday afternoon they took a boat to visit the calanques, those long coves with white cliffs plunging into turquoise water. Rose-Hélène loved the boat. Ioana, much less. After ten minutes she turned very pale and spent the rest of the trip sitting at the stern, her eyes fixed on the horizon.

“It’s seasickness,” Julien said, worried. “Do you want me to ask the captain to turn back?” Ioana shook her head. “No, it’ll pass.” She looked as if she wanted to say something else, but she kept quiet. Julien, busy stopping Rose-Hélène from leaning overboard, noticed nothing. He was a conductor, not a detective.

On Thursday 15 May, in the evening, after dinner, they went back down to the beach with the pushchair. Rose-Hélène fell asleep in two minutes, exhausted by her day of waves. The sun was setting behind the cliffs of Cap Canaille, which turned red, then purple. There was almost no one around. Just a fisherman, far off on the jetty, and the lighthouse that had just come on.

At last they talked about the ministry, as they had promised each other. Julien explained everything: the one-year contract, the office in Lyon, the four or five days of travel a month, Théo and Lucia for La Duchère, his post kept at the Conservatoire just in case. Ioana listened without interrupting, drawing lines in the sand with a stick, like an architect’s plan.

Then she told him she had weighed the pros and cons for three weeks, and there was only one con: he would be tired, and in a few months they would need him not to be. Julien asked why. And Ioana, putting her hand on her belly, replied that in case he hadn’t noticed, she hadn’t drunk coffee for two weeks.

Julien sat motionless for a long time. Then he looked at Ioana’s belly, then at her face, then at the morning’s boat rocking in the harbour, then at her belly again. “The seasickness,” he murmured at last. “It wasn’t seasickness.” Ioana laughed. “Well done, detective.” And Julien, the great conductor, began to cry like a child, sitting in the sand.

Rose-Hélène woke up at that very moment, as if she had sensed that something important was happening. She looked at her father with big eyes. “Why is Daddy crying?” she asked, in the serious voice she used for all her questions. Ioana took her on her lap. “Daddy is crying because he’s very happy. You’re going to have a little brother or a little sister.”

Rose-Hélène thought for a long time. You could almost see the questions forming in her little head. Then she asked the only one that really mattered to her: “Will he play the harmonica?” Ioana and Julien burst out laughing at the same time. Julien replied yes, as long as she agreed to lend him Henri’s from time to time. Rose-Hélène clutched the harmonica to her chest, very tightly. It was far from certain.

That evening, in the little house above the harbour, they did calculations on a paper napkin. If Ioana was six weeks pregnant, the baby was due around the beginning of January. “A winter baby,” Ioana said. “Like me.” Julien calculated something else: by the time of the birth, he would have planted at least five lime trees in five cities. He decided not to say so.

The next morning they called Odile. She picked up on the first ring, as if she had been waiting for the call. Ioana had barely begun her sentence when Odile interrupted her. “I know, my dear. I’ve known for three weeks. You refused my coffee twice, and you pulled a funny face at my sardines. At my age, you don’t get these things wrong any more.”

The grandmother, in Iași, reacted in exactly the same way. She had gone back to Romania a week earlier, on Costel’s coach, with an empty cool box and a full heart. When Ioana told her the news, she simply said she already knew, because she had dreamed of fish three nights in a row. In Romania, she explained, dreaming of fish never lies.

Elena cried on the phone for ten minutes, then started a new list. She asked whether the baby would be born in Lyon or Iași, whether she should come in December or January, and whether Ioana had remembered to buy vitamins. Dan only took the phone at the end to say, in the French of his old textbook: “All my congratulations, my dear daughter.”

On Friday, Julien wanted to make a detour through Marseille before going home. He wanted to show Rose-Hélène something. They parked the car above a little calanque, in the Les Goudes district, and walked down to a white house with blue shutters. The shutters were closed. A sign said the house was now a holiday let.

“This was the house of my grandfather Marcel and my grandmother Rose,” Julien explained to his daughter, who surely didn’t understand everything. “Your name comes from her. My grandfather played the accordion on this terrace, and my grandmother danced. They danced every evening, even when they were very old.” Rose-Hélène looked at the empty terrace. Then she blew three notes on the harmonica.

Ioana, looking at the house, thought of something. Julien’s grandparents had loved each other by the sea. Henri and Hélène had loved each other under a lime tree. Her own parents had got engaged under a walnut tree, and so had she. And Radu and Lucia had left the day before for Iași, to go and see that same walnut tree. There was always a tree, or the sea, somewhere in this family’s love stories.

It was on the terrace of a little café in Les Goudes, facing the sea, that Julien called Catherine Dumas. He put her on speaker so that Ioana could hear. He said he accepted, on condition that all the conditions they had discussed appeared in the contract. He added that there was a new one: he would not travel during the first week of January, unless the ministry burned down.

Catherine Dumas laughed. She didn’t ask why. She only said: “Congratulations, Mr Moreau.” Then she announced a piece of news that made Julien smile: the first lime tree planting would take place in Marseille, in October, in front of a music school in the Estaque district. A few kilometres from the house with blue shutters.

On Saturday, Mrs Giraud came to say goodbye with a second basket of figs, “in case you get hungry on the train”. She kissed Rose-Hélène on both cheeks and put her hand on Ioana’s belly, without asking anything. She had guessed too. “Come back next year,” she said. “As long as I’m still here. At my age you don’t promise anything any more, but you hope.”

On the train home, Rose-Hélène fell asleep on her father’s lap, the harmonica in one hand and a shell in the other. Ioana watched the vineyards of the Rhône valley go by. Julien took out his notebook. Under the date of 15 May, he wrote three words: “Sea. Yes. Baby.” Then he closed the notebook. For once he had nothing else to write down.

They got back to Lyon on Sunday evening. On Monday, Julien went to La Duchère to announce the news officially to the children. He explained that from September, Théo and Lucia would conduct the orchestra three days a week, and that he would come on Wednesdays and Saturdays. The children applauded Théo, who turned red to the ears.

Lucia, who had just come back from Romania with Radu, told them about the walnut tree, the hill, the village, the grandmother’s mămăligă, and the moment when Radu, under the tree, finally read Hélène’s letter aloud. The children listened in silence. Then Inès raised her hand. She had heard about the baby from her mother, who had heard from Mrs Mansouri, who had heard from Odile.

“Sir,” she asked, “if it’s a boy, will he play the clarinet?” Julien replied that he didn’t know yet, that they’d have to ask him once he was born. Inès thought about it. “In case he wants to,” she said very seriously, “I could teach him. As long as he’s patient.” Julien wrote the offer in his notebook, with the date.

That evening, Ioana bought a little blue notebook at the stationer’s on rue d’Austerlitz. On the first page she wrote: “Just in case”. Then she started a list: Rose-Hélène’s clothes to keep, the cot to put back together, the room to repaint, a boy’s name, a girl’s name. For the girl’s name she left a blank line. For the boy’s name too.

Rose-Hélène, looking over her shoulder, put her finger on the blank line. “Baby Waltz,” she said, with great authority. Ioana laughed, but she wrote it anyway, in pencil, just in case. Outside, on the landing, you could hear Odile softly whistling the first three notes, as every evening before bed. That evening, for the first time, Ioana had the feeling that someone, deep inside her, was listening too.

The ministry sends Julien the draft contract. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.

Article 1. Mr Julien Moreau is appointed national coordinator of the “Musique en partage” network, from 1 July 2030, for a renewable period of one year, on condition that the first year’s assessment is judged satisfactory.

Article 2. The coordinator will carry out his duties from an office located in Lyon. He will visit the partner cities at least once a quarter, unless exceptional circumstances prevent him from doing so.

Article 3. Should the coordinator wish to end the contract before its term, he must inform the ministry with three months’ notice. His post at the Lyon Conservatoire will be kept for him for twelve months.
Article 4. The coordinator may continue to conduct the La Duchère orchestra two days a week, provided that this activity does not harm his national duties.
Article 5. Each partner city undertakes to provide a rehearsal hall and, as far as possible, to plant a lime tree in front of it. Should a city have no green space, a tree in a pot will be accepted.

Julien read article 5 three times. Then he called Catherine Dumas to ask her who had come up with the idea of the lime trees. “A certain Madame Bernard,” she replied. “She wrote me a four-page letter. If you ever see her, thank her for me.”
